passages.title: The oath by time and the four saving qualities
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

In three short ayat Allah swears an oath by *time*, declares that mankind is in a state of loss, and then makes an exception for people who are characterized by four qualities together — faith, righteous deeds, advising each other for truth, and advising each other for patience. That is the whole architecture. Ayah 1 is the oath, ayah 2 is the verdict, ayah 3 is the exception. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it "a concise but comprehensive Surah, which in three verses, outlines a complete way of human life based on the Islamic worldview," and says this is "the only path to salvation in this world, as well as in the next world."

---

## The imitation that convinced no one

Ibn Kathir opens his commentary not with grammar but with a story, and it is worth telling properly.

They have mentioned that ʿAmr bin al-ʿAs went to visit Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab — this was after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been commissioned as a Prophet, and before ʿAmr had accepted Islam. On arriving, Musaylimah asked him, "What has been revealed to your friend during this time?" ʿAmr said that a short and concise surah had been revealed to him. Musaylimah asked what it was, and ʿAmr recited: *By al-ʿAsr. Verily, man is in loss. Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and recommend one another to the truth, and recommend one another to patience.*

Musaylimah thought for a while. Then he said, "Indeed something similar has also been revealed to me." ʿAmr asked what it was. Musaylimah produced: "O Wabr, O Wabr! You are only two ears and a chest, and the rest of you is digging and burrowing." The *wabr*, Ibn Kathir explains, is a small animal that resembles a cat — a small, furry mammal, the hyrax — and the largest things on it are its ears and its torso, while the rest of it is ugly.

Then Musaylimah asked, "What do you think, O ʿAmr?" And ʿAmr — who had not yet accepted Islam — replied: **"By Allah! Verily, you know that I know you are lying."**

Ibn Kathir adds a note of scholarly care that is itself instructive: he says he saw that Abu Bakr al-Kharaʼiti mentioned a chain of narration for part of this story, or what was close to its meaning, in volume two of his famous book *Masawiʼ ul-Akhlaq*. Musaylimah, Ibn Kathir concludes, intended by the composition of those nonsensical verses to produce something that would oppose the Qur'an — "yet, it was not even convincing to the idol worshipper of that time."

Keep that scene in mind as you read the three ayat. Their compression is not simplicity. A man setting out to compose something that could stand against them managed only that.

## "It would be sufficient for them"

Two more reports frame how this surah was received.

At-Tabarani recorded from ʿAbdullah bin Hisn Abi Madinah (named in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as ʿUbaidullah Ibn Hisn) that **whenever two men from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to meet, they would not part until one of them had recited Surat al-ʿAsr in its entirety to the other, and one of them had given the greetings of peace to the other.**

Sit with what that habit means. The surah's own final command is that people *advise one another* to truth and to patience. In this practice of the Companions, no parting happened without the whole surah being said aloud between them.

And Imam Ash-Shafiʿi said: **"If the people were to ponder on this Surah, it would be sufficient for them."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: if people thought about Surah al-ʿAsr carefully, it would be enough for their guidance.

---

## Ayah 1: the oath — what is *al-ʿAsr*?

Allah swears: **وَٱلۡعَصۡرِ** — *By al-ʿAsr.*

Ibn Kathir reports two positions:

- **Al-ʿAsr is time itself** — "the time in which the movements of the Children of Adam occur, whether good or evil." That is, the whole medium in which human action unfolds.
- **"It is the evening"** — narrated by Malik from Zayd bin Aslam.

Ibn Kathir states plainly that **the first view is the popular opinion**, and the commentary proceeds on that basis. Both are transmitted views of respected early figures; the reader should know that the difference exists and where the weight of opinion falls.

## Why swear by *time* in particular?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this the heart of its commentary. Its starting principle: **there needs to be a relationship between an oath and its subject.** So what is the link between *time* and *man is in loss*?

**First answer: time is the arena.** The commentators generally state that all the conditions of man — his growth and development, his movements, his actions and morality — take place within the space of time. Swearing by time is swearing by the very medium his life is made of.

**Second answer, and the one Maʿārif develops: time is a capital that drains away.** "Hours, days, months, and years of life pass quickly, spiritual and material potentialities decline, and abilities fade. Man is like a person who possesses great capital and, without his permission and will, every day, a portion of that capital is taken away. This is the nature of life in this world; the nature of continual loss."

The commentary quotes a line of Arabic poetry that puts it exactly:

> **"Your life comprises a few breaths that can be counted; when one of them is sent out, a part of your life has diminished."**

**The trader and the melting capital.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the image. Allah has granted man the invaluable capital of his life so that he may invest it in a profitable business venture. Invest it sensibly in good works and there will be no limit to the profitable returns. Invest it unwisely in evil works and, far from attracting returns, he loses the capital *and* incurs the dreadful scourge of committing numerous sins. And if a person invests his life-capital in neither good deeds nor evil deeds, **he at least loses both the profit and the capital.**

This is not merely poetic imagery, Maʿārif insists; it is supported by a Prophetic hadith, according to which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is reported to have said that **when a person wakes up in the morning, he invests his soul or life in a business enterprise: some of the investors free or save the capital from loss, and others destroy it.** (The commentary quotes this teaching of the Prophet ﷺ without naming the collection it comes from, so it is passed on here as the commentary gives it.)

And the Qur'an itself uses the word *tijarah* — trade — in relation to faith and righteous deeds: *"...shall I tell you about a trade that saves you from a painful punishment?"* (61:10).

Since time is man's capital of life, says Maʿārif, **the man himself is the trader.** And under normal circumstances his capital is not a frozen thing that may be kept for a while and used up later when the need arises; it is fluid, flowing all the time, every minute and every second. The one who invests it needs to be very wise, intelligent and agile, so that he can swiftly reap profit from a flowing capital.

Then comes the detail that makes the image bite. **One of the old scholars said he had learnt the meaning of this verse from an ice-seller**, whose trade required utmost diligence, because if he were neglectful for a moment his entire capital would melt away. That, says Maʿārif, is why this verse swears an oath by time: to indicate that it is **melting capital**, and that the only way to escape loss is to take every moment of one's life as valuable and use it for the four acts mentioned in the surah.

**Third answer: history itself testifies.** Maʿārif offers a further possible reason — time, in the sense of *history*, bears testimony to the fact mentioned in the surah. If one thinks about the causes of the rise and decline of individuals and nations, he would certainly come to believe that it is only these four acts that ensure the real success and betterment of mankind, and that whoever abandoned them suffered a great loss, "as is evident from numerous events recorded by history."

---

## Ayah 2: "Verily, man is in loss"

**إِنَّ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ لَفِي خُسۡرٍ.** Ibn Kathir glosses *khusr* as **"loss and destruction"** — Allah swears by al-ʿAsr that man is in *khusr*, which means in loss and destruction.

Note the framing Ibn Kathir uses when he moves to the next ayah: Allah "makes an exception, among the species of man being in loss." The state described belongs to the human *species*; those who are saved are the exception carved out of it, not the assumed baseline.

## Ayah 3: the four qualities

**Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and recommend one another to the truth, and recommend one another to patience.**

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the first two is beautifully economical: the exception is for **"those who believe in their hearts and work righteous deeds with their limbs."** Inward and outward, together.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir, points out the shape of the four: **the first two relate to man's own personal betterment, and the other two relate to other people's guidance and reform.** Maʿārif adds that faith and righteous deeds concern man's moral and spiritual growth and are not in need of elaboration; it is the last two that require some explanation.

### *Tawāsī* — the word to feel

The word rendered "recommend one another" or "advising each other" is *tawāsī*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it up: the infinitive **tawāsī is derived from *wasiyyah*, which means "to advise somebody strongly and effectively about the best thing to do in a particular situation."** The term *wasiyyah* also refers to a **will or testament**, where a testator advises his executor regarding the disposal of his estate on his death.

That is the register: strong, effective advice, carrying the weight of a last instruction. And because the form is *tawāsī* — mutual — it is believers pressing this on one another, back and forth.

Maʿārif calls the two clauses **"two chapters of the same testament":** advice to truth, and advice to patience and fortitude.

### *Haqq* and *sabr* — how the scholars read them

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says these two concepts may be explained in different ways, and offers them as genuine alternatives rather than settling the matter:

- **Reading one:** *haqq* (truth) refers to the package of correct faith and good deeds, while *sabr* (patience) refers to abstinence from all sins and evil deeds. On this reading the first clause refers to **enjoining good actions** and the second to **forbidding evil actions**. The cumulative sense, Maʿārif says, is that believers are enjoined not only to adopt right faith and good deeds themselves, but to advise others strongly and effectively to adopt them, and so help create a healthy atmosphere around them.
- **Reading two:** *haqq* refers to the articles of faith, while *sabr* refers to all good actions together with abstinence from evil deeds. This leans on the root sense: **the word *sabr* originally means "to withhold oneself and to bind oneself,"** which encompasses binding oneself down to the performance of righteous deeds and abstaining from sins.

Ibn Kathir glosses them somewhat differently again. For him, "recommend one another to the truth" is **"to perform acts of obedience and avoid the forbidden things,"** while "recommend one another to patience" means patience **"with the plots, the evils, and the harms of those who harm people due to their commanding them to do good and forbidding them from evil."** On his reading, the fourth quality is tied directly to the third: calling others to good and warning them from evil draws harm, and *sabr* is borne with precisely that.

### Ibn Taymiyyah: the two things that hold a person back

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Hafiz Ibn Taymiyyah stated in one of his monographs that there are normally **two factors that restrain a person from faith and righteous deeds:**

1. **Doubts about the true faith.** When such doubts arise in people's minds, they destroy faith and leave a person confused and confounded, and this in turn adversely affects his righteous deeds.
2. **Selfish desires,** which stop a man from doing good and involve him in evil. Here he theoretically believes he should do good and abstain from sins, but his selfish desires lead him to stray from the right path.

And the ayah, says Maʿārif, indicates the removal of both. **"Advice of truth"** caters to the first — it is to be removed by reforming others on the theoretical and academic level. **"Advice of patience"** takes care of the second, by enjoining Muslims to advise others to give up base desires and remain firm against their evil demands. Put differently: enjoining truth means **improving the knowledge of Muslims, their intellectual development**; enjoining patience means **improving their practical life.**

---

## Living it: you cannot be saved alone

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion under the heading *Need to Salvage the Entire Muslim Society*, and it is blunt.

The surah lays down the important principle that **inviting other Muslims to keep to the true faith and good deeds is as much a necessity as one's own submission to the Holy Qur'an and Sunnah.** Without sincere efforts, to the best of one's ability, to invite others to the right path, one's own good deeds are not enough for one's salvation.

It then applies this where it stings most: **especially if a person does not take care of the spiritual and moral welfare of his wife, children and family, and turns a blind eye to their unrighteous deeds, he is blocking his way to salvation — no matter how pious he himself might be.** Therefore, it says, the Qur'an and the Sunnah make it obligatory upon every Muslim to do his best to invite others to good deeds and warn them against evil acts.

And the complaint is not aimed only at the general public: Maʿārif observes that, let alone the general public, **many learned people are lax in this matter**, thinking it sufficient to be concerned about their own moral and spiritual well-being while unconcerned about the well-being of their family and children. The section closes with a supplication — *may Allah grant us the ability to act upon this verse* — which is the right note. This is a demand, not a boast.

---

## Holding it together

Read the three ayat as one movement. Allah swears by time — the capital that is flowing away every minute and every second (ayah 1). He states that mankind is in a state of loss (ayah 2). He then names the four qualities that are the exception (ayah 3): believing in the heart, working righteous deeds with the limbs, and then advising one another — strongly and effectively, as a man advises in his will — to truth and to patience.

The first two are your own betterment. The last two are the guidance and reform of others, and without sincere effort at them your own good deeds are not enough for your salvation. And the Companions, on this understanding, would not part from one another until the whole surah had been recited between them.
